## BROWSER-01 HSTS sent with a long max-age and includeSubDomains

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-319, CWE-523 · OWASP A02:2021, A05:2021, A02:2025, A04:2025, API8:2023 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Without HSTS, a user typing the bare domain on hostile Wi-Fi makes a first HTTP request that an active attacker can downgrade (SSL stripping) to read session cookies or inject script. Vercel's default on custom domains omits includeSubDomains, so sibling subdomains and parent-domain cookies stay exposed.

### Build rule

Send `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains` on every HTTPS response from the apex and www, set in `next.config` `headers()` for `/(.*)` or in `vercel.json`, after confirming every subdomain serves HTTPS. Add `preload` only as a deliberate owner decision: hstspreload.org says inclusion cannot easily be undone and asks tools not to add it by default. HTTP to HTTPS redirects are INFRA-01.

### Proof test

1. The tool fetches the home page over HTTPS, following same-origin redirects, and every HTML page the crawl reaches (up to `--max-pages`, default 25); the report names the worst page.
2. It reads the `Strict-Transport-Security` response header on each.
3. Pass: header present with `max-age` of at least 31536000 and `includeSubDomains` on every page.
4. Fail: header missing, `max-age` below one year, or a directive repeated (RFC 6797 makes the header invalid, so browsers ignore it). Warning: no `includeSubDomains` (a weaker setting, not a proven flaw: it matters when subdomains or parent-domain cookies exist).
5. Manual extra: repeat for `https://www.<domain>/`; if preload is intended, check status at hstspreload.org.

### Sources

- [RFC 6797: HTTP Strict Transport Security](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6797)
- [Vercel docs: Encryption and TLS (default HSTS)](https://vercel.com/docs/security/encryption)
- [HSTS preload list submission requirements](https://hstspreload.org/)
- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-02 Content-Security-Policy without unsafe-inline scripts

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-693, CWE-79 · OWASP A03:2021, A05:2021, A02:2025, A05:2025, API8:2023 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any, nextjs

### Risk

Without an enforcing CSP, any injection bug (BROWSER-09 to BROWSER-11) runs script in the site's origin. `'unsafe-inline'` without a nonce or hash gives no XSS protection, host allowlists are usually bypassable, and a Report-Only policy blocks nothing. Google's study of about 1.68M hosts found 94.72% of distinct CSPs trivially bypassable.

### Build rule

For dynamic App Router pages, build the policy in `proxy.ts` (`middleware.ts` before Next.js 16) with a fresh nonce per request (`Buffer.from(crypto.randomUUID()).toString('base64')`) and set it on both the request headers and the response. Baseline from the Next.js docs: `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-<N>' 'strict-dynamic'; style-src 'self' 'nonce-<N>'; img-src 'self' blob: data:; font-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; upgrade-insecure-requests`. Add `connect-src` for the Supabase project URL (https and wss) and analytics hosts. Allow `'unsafe-eval'` only when `NODE_ENV === 'development'`. Pass `nonce` to every `<Script>`. Fully static sites use `experimental.sri` with a `script-src` that has no `'unsafe-inline'` (the Next.js SRI example). The static `next.config` policy in the Next.js guide's "Without Nonces" section includes `'unsafe-inline'` and does not pass this check. Roll out as Report-Only first, then enforce.

### Proof test

1. The tool fetches the home page, following same-origin redirects, and every HTML page the crawl reaches (up to `--max-pages`, default 25); the report names the worst page and how many pages share the result. On each it reads the enforcing `Content-Security-Policy` header (not `-Report-Only`) and any `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` policy, without the directives browsers ignore in a meta tag (`frame-ancestors`, `report-uri`, `sandbox`).
2. For `<script>` elements it takes `script-src-elem`, else `script-src`, else `default-src`; for inline event handlers `script-src-attr`, else `script-src`, else `default-src` (CSP3 fallback order). Several enforcing policies all apply, so a script must be allowed by every one of them, and the strictest policy decides.
3. Pass: an enforcing policy is set and its script directive has no `'unsafe-inline'`, or has it only alongside a `'nonce-...'` or `'sha256-'`/`'sha384-'`/`'sha512-'` source, and allows no source that matches every host (`*`, a bare scheme such as `https:`, `http:` or `data:`, `https://*`, or `*.com`) unless `'strict-dynamic'` is set with a nonce or hash.
4. Fail: no enforcing CSP (including report-only CSP without an enforcing policy), no script directive in any policy, `'unsafe-inline'` with no nonce or hash in the element or attribute directive, a source that matches every host, or a nonce that repeats: when the home page's policy has a nonce, the tool fetches it once more and fails if the same nonce comes back.
5. Manual extra: confirm `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri`, no `'unsafe-eval'` in production, and zero CSP violations in the browser console on key pages.

### Sources

- [W3C CSP3: Report-Only header](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/#csp-report-only-header)
- [Next.js docs: How to set a Content Security Policy](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/content-security-policy)
- [Weichselbaum et al., CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP (CCS 2016)](https://research.google/pubs/csp-is-dead-long-live-csp-on-the-insecurity-of-whitelists-and-the-future-of-content-security-policy/)
- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-03 X-Content-Type-Options set to nosniff

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-430 · OWASP A05:2021, A02:2025, API8:2023 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Without `nosniff`, browsers may guess a response's type and run an uploaded file or JSON body as HTML or script. On the app's own origin that becomes same-origin XSS or hosted phishing content.

### Build rule

Send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on all responses (`next.config` `headers()` for `/(.*)` or `vercel.json`). Every response also carries a correct `Content-Type`; HTML includes `charset=utf-8`. Upload handling is BROWSER-13.

### Proof test

1. The tool fetches the home page, following same-origin redirects, and every HTML page the crawl reaches (up to `--max-pages`, default 25); the report names the worst page and how many pages share the result.
2. Pass: `X-Content-Type-Options` equals `nosniff` on every page.
3. Fail: header missing or any other value.
4. Manual extra: `curl -sI` an API route and a static asset and confirm the same header.

### Sources

- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [OWASP Secure Headers Project](https://owasp.org/www-project-secure-headers/)

## BROWSER-04 Clickjacking protection with frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-1021 · OWASP A05:2021, A02:2025, API8:2023 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any

### Risk

If pages can be framed by another origin, an attacker page can overlay them and trick a logged-in user into clicking buttons such as delete account or approve access. The February 2009 Twitter "Don't Click" worm used clickjacking to make users re-post the malicious link.

### Build rule

Send CSP `frame-ancestors 'none'` (or `'self'` if the app frames itself) on all HTML responses, plus `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or `SAMEORIGIN`) for older browsers. If a widget must be embeddable, list exact origins in `frame-ancestors` for that route only. `frame-ancestors` is ignored in a `<meta>` CSP; it must be an HTTP header.

### Proof test

1. The tool fetches the home page, following same-origin redirects, and every HTML page the crawl reaches (up to `--max-pages`, default 25); the report names the worst page and how many pages share the result.
2. Pass on every page: the CSP header contains `frame-ancestors` with `'none'`, `'self'` or an explicit origin list, or `X-Frame-Options` is `DENY` or `SAMEORIGIN`.
3. Fail: neither is present, or every `frame-ancestors` allows any site (`*` or a bare scheme). When several policies set `frame-ancestors`, the most restrictive one applies. `frame-ancestors` in a `<meta>` tag does not count, because browsers ignore it there.
4. Manual extra: repeat on login, settings and destructive-action pages; optionally frame one from a localhost page and confirm the browser refuses to render it.

### Sources

- [OWASP: Clickjacking](https://wiki.owasp.org/index.php/Clickjacking)
- [The Register: Twitter clickjack attack (2009)](https://www.theregister.com/2009/02/13/twitter_clickjack_attack/)
- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-05 Referrer-Policy limits what leaks to other sites

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-200, CWE-598 · OWASP A05:2021, A02:2025, API8:2023 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Without a strict Referrer-Policy, the full URL of a page, including reset, invite or auth codes in the query string, is sent in the `Referer` header to every third-party resource and outbound link. The token-flow test is BROWSER-16.

### Build rule

Send `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` site-wide (OWASP cheat sheet value) and `no-referrer` on auth callback, reset and invite routes.

### Proof test

1. The tool fetches the home page, following same-origin redirects, and every HTML page the crawl reaches (up to `--max-pages`, default 25); the report names the worst page and how many pages share the result.
2. Pass on every page: `Referrer-Policy` is `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `strict-origin`, `same-origin` or `no-referrer`. Repeated fields are one list: the last recognised token wins, and an unknown token is ignored.
3. Fail: `unsafe-url` or `no-referrer-when-downgrade`. Warning: header missing (modern browsers default to `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`), `origin` or `origin-when-cross-origin`.

### Sources

- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [OWASP Secure Headers Project recommended headers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OWASP/www-project-secure-headers/master/ci/headers_add.json)

## BROWSER-06 Cookies set with Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-614, CWE-1004, CWE-1275 · OWASP A05:2021, A07:2021, A02:2025, A07:2025, API8:2023 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

A cookie without `Secure` can travel over plain HTTP; a session cookie without `HttpOnly` can be read by any injected script; a cookie without `SameSite` is sent on cross-site requests, which feeds CSRF. Post-login auth cookies are BROWSER-17.

### Build rule

Every cookie the app sets carries `Secure` in production and an explicit `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`). App-owned session and CSRF cookies also carry `HttpOnly`, use the `__Host-` prefix with `Path=/`, and have no `Domain`. Use `SameSite=None` only for a documented cross-site need, and always with `Secure`.

### Proof test

1. The tool fetches the home page, following same-origin redirects, and every page the crawl reaches (up to `--max-pages`, default 25), and reads every `Set-Cookie`.
2. On https, each cookie must have `Secure`.
3. Cookies whose names look like sessions must have `HttpOnly`. A name counts when one of its words (split on punctuation and camelCase, after any `__Host-` or `__Secure-` prefix) is session, sess, sid, sessionid, auth, token, jwt, login, remember or refresh, or starts with sess or ssess, contains session, or ends with auth or token (`.ASPXAUTH`, `ASPSESSIONID...`, Drupal `SESS...`, `MOODLESESSION`, `CFTOKEN`), so `author`, `authorized` or `consider` do not count. Double-submit CSRF cookies (`csrftoken`, `XSRF-TOKEN`, `_csrf`, `csrf_token`) are exempt: JavaScript must read them by design.
4. Each cookie must have an explicit `SameSite` attribute.
5. Pass: all rules hold and at least one session cookie (by the name rule above) was observed. Manual: cookies were set but none looks like a session cookie, so the cookie this check is for was not seen; log in with a test account and check it. A session cookie with an unusual name is judged like any other cookie. Fail: a Secure or HttpOnly rule is broken; the report names the cookie. A cookie with no `SameSite` is a warning, because browsers default it to Lax. No cookies on any crawled page is reported as not applicable; log in with a test account and repeat on the session cookie.

### Sources

- [MDN: Set-Cookie](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie)
- [OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-07 CORS does not reflect arbitrary origins with credentials

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-942, CWE-346 · OWASP A01:2021, A05:2021, A01:2025, A02:2025, API8:2023 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any, nextjs, node

### Risk

Route handlers often echo `request.headers.get('origin')` into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, which lets any website make logged-in requests and read the answer. PortSwigger Research documented a bitcoin exchange whose look-alike-domain origin check let an attacker read wallet backups, and a site leaking users' API keys the same way.

### Build rule

Prefer no CORS: a Next.js front end and its route handlers are same-origin. If cross-origin access is required, compare the Origin against an exact allowlist of full origins (scheme, host, port) from config, set `Vary: Origin`, never reflect arbitrary values, never allow `null`, never use regex or `endsWith` matching, and never combine `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` with `*` or reflection. Public read-only endpoints may use `*` without credentials. Supabase's REST API uses `*` by design with bearer JWT and RLS; do not copy that to cookie-authenticated routes.

### Proof test

1. The tool sends one GET per test origin to the home page and to up to 3 API-looking routes the crawl found (`/api`, `/graphql`, `/trpc`, `/rest` paths in links, form actions, the login endpoint and inline-script strings) per test origin: `https://asa-origin-probe.invalid` (reserved TLD, never a real host), `null`, `https://<yourhost>.asa-origin-probe.invalid` (an allowlist that checks "starts with"), `https://asa-origin-probe-<yourhost>` (one that checks "ends with") and `https://asa-origin-probe.<yourhost>` (a subdomain). The origins are header values only; nothing is sent to them.
2. Fail: the response echoes any of the first four in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
3. Warning: one of them is echoed without credentials, or the subdomain origin is echoed with credentials (safe only if every subdomain is trusted).
4. Pass: otherwise, with at least one API route answering (not 404 or 405). Manual: no API route was found or answered, because CORS is usually set on API routes rather than the home page.
5. Manual extra: repeat against the remaining API routes and an OPTIONS preflight. Read-only requests only.

### Sources

- [PortSwigger Research: Exploiting CORS misconfigurations for Bitcoins and bounties](https://portswigger.net/research/exploiting-cors-misconfigurations-for-bitcoins-and-bounties)
- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-08 Permissions-Policy and Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy set

Severity: low · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-693, CWE-1021 · OWASP A05:2021, A02:2025, API8:2023 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Without `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy`, windows the site opens or is opened by keep a `window` reference, enabling XS-Leaks and reverse tabnabbing. Without `Permissions-Policy`, an injected script or third-party iframe can prompt for camera, microphone, location or payment under the site's name.

### Build rule

Send `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` (`same-origin-allow-popups` if the app uses OAuth or payment popups) and `Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=(), usb=(), browsing-topics=()`, allowing only features the app uses (e.g. `camera=(self)`). Send `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site` on API and user-file responses. Send `X-XSS-Protection: 0` or omit it; do not send `Expect-CT`. Do not set `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` by default. Hiding `X-Powered-By` is NEXT-03.

### Proof test

1. The tool fetches the home page, following same-origin redirects, and every HTML page the crawl reaches (up to `--max-pages`, default 25); the report names the worst page and how many pages share the result.
2. Pass on every page: `Permissions-Policy` is present and the complete combined `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` field parses as a case-sensitive `same-origin` or `same-origin-allow-popups` token item. Parameters such as `report-to="endpoint"` are allowed; the check validates string, token, boolean and numeric parameter syntax, not reporting delivery.
3. Warning: either header missing or the parsed COOP token is outside those two values. An unvalidated item (including malformed syntax, duplicate/list values, unsupported parameter types, or a value over 8192 characters) needs manual review and cannot pass. Byte sequence, date and display string parameters are not parsed by this check.
4. Manual extra: confirm any unvalidated COOP header follows the structured field syntax. If the app uses popups, run the OAuth or payment popup flow once on staging and confirm it still completes.

### Sources

- [HTML Standard: Cross-origin opener policy headers](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#the-cross-origin-opener-policy-header)
- [RFC 9651: Parsing Structured Fields](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9651.html#section-4.2)
- [MDN: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy)
- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [OWASP Secure Headers Project recommended headers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OWASP/www-project-secure-headers/master/ci/headers_add.json)

## BROWSER-09 No unsanitized HTML through dangerouslySetInnerHTML or innerHTML

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-79 · OWASP A03:2021, A05:2025 · Mode: review (code audit built in: `asa code`) · Stacks: any, nextjs

### Risk

React escapes text by default, so in Next.js apps XSS almost always enters through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `innerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML` or `document.write` fed with user, CMS, LLM or database content. Script in the page can read JS-readable tokens (Supabase session cookies by default) and act as the user, which also defeats every CSRF defense. GHSA-m7qm-r2r5-f77q was a high-severity XSS in react-marked-markdown.

### Build rule

Do not use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for anything not authored by the developer at build time. If rich HTML is required, sanitize with DOMPurify (`isomorphic-dompurify` on the server) using an allowlist profile, at render time, next to the sink; do not trust "sanitized on write" data other writers can reach. Never pass user input to `innerHTML`, `eval`, `new Function` or `setTimeout(string)`. JSON in `<script>` tags (JSON-LD) must escape `<` (`JSON.stringify(x).replace(/</g, '\u003c')`). Strict CSP (BROWSER-02) is the second layer.

### Proof test

1. Grep the repo for `dangerouslySetInnerHTML|innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document.write|new Function`.
2. For each hit, confirm the value is a constant or the direct output of a sanitizer.
3. Optional, own test account: save an inert canary such as `<b data-asa-canary="1">asa</b>` into each rich-text field and query the rendered DOM for `[data-asa-canary]`.
4. Pass: every sink is constant or sanitized, and the canary renders as text or with the `data-` attribute stripped.
5. Fail: any sink takes unsanitized dynamic data, or the canary element appears with its attributes intact.

### Sources

- [GHSA-m7qm-r2r5-f77q: react-marked-markdown XSS](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m7qm-r2r5-f77q)
- [OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet (XSS defeats CSRF defenses)](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-10 User-supplied links and navigations allow only safe URL schemes

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-79, CWE-83 · OWASP A03:2021, A05:2025 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any, nextjs

### Risk

Profile website fields, CMS links and `?returnTo=` values often reach `href`, `router.push`, `window.location` or `window.open`. A `javascript:` URL runs as code in the site's origin when clicked or navigated. React 19 blocks it in React-rendered attributes, but `window.location`, `location.assign`, `window.open` and non-React DOM code are not covered.

### Build rule

Parse every user-supplied URL with `new URL(value, base)` and allow only `https:` (and `http:`, `mailto:`, `tel:` when needed) by exact `protocol` match; reject anything else at write time and again at render time. Never use `startsWith('http')` checks. Enable the lint rule `react/jsx-no-script-url`. Apply the same check before `window.location` or `window.open`. Stay on React 19 or later.

### Proof test

1. Repo: grep for `href={`, `router.push(`, `location.href =`, `location.assign(`, `window.open(` with non-literal arguments; confirm a scheme allowlist guards each.
2. Own test account: try to save a link field with a `javascript:` scheme and with a `data:text/html` scheme.
3. Pass: the server rejects with 4xx or stores a neutralized value, and the rendered anchor's `href` does not use that scheme.
4. Fail: the value round-trips into an anchor or navigation sink. Never click the stored link.

### Sources

- [React 16.9 release notes (javascript: URL deprecation)](https://legacy.reactjs.org/blog/2019/08/08/react-v16.9.0.html)

## BROWSER-11 Markdown renderers do not pass raw HTML unsanitized

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-79 · OWASP A03:2021, A05:2025 · Mode: review · Stacks: any, nextjs

### Risk

Comments, bios, AI chat output and docs are often rendered with react-markdown, marked or markdown-it. react-markdown escapes HTML by default, but adding `rehype-raw`, or marked/markdown-it with `html: true` piped into `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, passes raw HTML and link schemes through. LLM output counts as user input because prompt injection can make the model emit markup.

### Build rule

Use react-markdown without `rehype-raw` for untrusted content. If raw HTML is required, put `rehype-sanitize` after `rehype-raw` in the plugin list. For marked or markdown-it, keep `html: false` and run output through DOMPurify before any HTML sink. Keep react-markdown's default `urlTransform`; never replace it with an identity function.

### Proof test

1. Read every markdown component's configuration.
2. Fail if `rehype-raw` appears without a later `rehype-sanitize`, if `urlTransform` is overridden to pass values through, or if marked/markdown-it output reaches `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` unsanitized.
3. Optional, own test account: post the BROWSER-09 canary plus a markdown link with a `javascript:` scheme; pass if the canary shows as text or stripped and the link has no `javascript:` href.

### Sources

- [rehype-raw README (XSS warning)](https://github.com/rehypejs/rehype-raw)
- [GHSA-m7qm-r2r5-f77q: react-marked-markdown XSS](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m7qm-r2r5-f77q)

## BROWSER-12 CSP nonce is fresh per response and never cached

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-330, CWE-693 · OWASP A03:2021, A05:2021, A02:2025, A05:2025 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: nextjs, vercel

### Risk

A nonce only works if an attacker cannot predict it. If nonce-bearing HTML is cached by the CDN, ISR or `Cache-Control: public`, every visitor gets the same nonce, which makes it no better than `'unsafe-inline'`. A header nonce that differs from the HTML nonce blocks the site's own scripts and tempts developers to loosen the policy.

### Build rule

Any route whose CSP contains `'nonce-` must be dynamically rendered (`await connection()`) and served with `Cache-Control: private, no-store`, or use Vercel's self-fetch pattern that injects a new nonce into cached HTML. Nonce CSP is incompatible with Partial Prerendering. Keep CDN-cached marketing pages on a static hash policy instead.

### Proof test

1. Request the same nonce-protected URL twice with `curl -si`.
2. Extract the `'nonce-...'` value from the CSP header and from `<script nonce=...>` in the body of each response.
3. Pass: nonces differ between the two responses and header matches body within each.
4. Fail: the same nonce twice, a header/body mismatch, or `x-vercel-cache: HIT` on a response with a nonce CSP.

### Sources

- [Vercel KB: CSP nonces with CDN cache](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/csp-nonces-with-cdn-cache)
- [Next.js docs: How to set a Content Security Policy](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/content-security-policy)

## BROWSER-13 User-uploaded files are never served as active content

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-430, CWE-79, CWE-434 · OWASP A03:2021, A04:2021, A05:2025, A06:2025 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any, nextjs, supabase

### Risk

Uploaded files served with the uploader's content type, or proxied through the app origin, can run as HTML or SVG script in the site's origin or host phishing pages under its name. CVE-2025-55173 let Next.js image optimization serve attacker-controlled content and filenames from external image sources (fixed in 14.2.31 and 15.4.5).

### Build rule

Route handlers that return files set `Content-Type` from a server-side allowlist (never the client-supplied type), send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (BROWSER-03), and send `Content-Disposition: attachment` for anything that is not an image. Restrict Supabase Storage bucket `allowed_mime_types` and reject HTML and SVG uploads unless sanitized. Keep `images.remotePatterns` narrow and Next.js patched.

### Proof test

1. With a test account, upload a harmless `.html` text file and a harmless `.svg` through every upload feature.
2. Fetch each stored file with `curl -sI` at the URL the app serves it from.
3. Pass: the upload is rejected, or it is served with `Content-Disposition: attachment` or a non-active type, plus `nosniff`.
4. Fail: the file is returned inline as `text/html` or `image/svg+xml` from the app origin.
5. Check the `next` version in the lockfile is at or above the patched line for CVE-2025-55173.

### Sources

- [GitLab advisory CVE-2025-55173: Next.js image optimization content injection](https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/npm/next/CVE-2025-55173/)
- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-14 Cookie-authenticated route handlers reject cross-site requests

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-352 · OWASP A01:2021, A01:2025 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: nextjs, supabase

### Risk

Next.js Server Actions compare Origin to Host, but custom `route.ts` POST, PUT and DELETE handlers and GET handlers with side effects get no built-in CSRF protection. `SameSite=Lax` leaves state-changing GETs and same-site subdomains exposed. CVE-2026-27978 let `Origin: null` from sandboxed iframes skip the Server Actions check in Next.js 16.0.1 to before 16.1.7.

### Build rule

Keep Next.js patched. Never change state in GET handlers or during render. In `proxy.ts` or a shared helper, reject non-safe methods when `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `cross-site`, with a fallback that requires `Origin` to equal the site origin; treat a missing or `null` Origin on a cookie-authenticated mutation as reject. Require `Content-Type: application/json` for JSON APIs. Never add `'null'` or wildcards to `serverActions.allowedOrigins`. Use `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` as defense in depth only. Webhooks skip origin checks but must verify signatures.

### Proof test

1. With a test account's session cookie, pick a harmless mutation (set own display name to its current value).
2. Send it with `Origin: https://asa-probe.invalid` and `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`; again with `Origin: null`; again with no Origin.
3. Control: send it with the correct Origin and confirm it succeeds.
4. Pass: all three probes get 4xx and the value is unchanged. Fail: any probe gets 2xx and the change applies.
5. Confirm `next` in the lockfile is at or above 16.1.7 (or the patched line for its major).

### Sources

- [OSV GHSA-mq59-m269-xvcx / CVE-2026-27978: Next.js null Origin bypasses Server Actions CSRF check](https://osv.dev/vulnerability/GHSA-mq59-m269-xvcx)
- [Next.js docs: How to think about data security](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/data-security)
- [OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-15 Login, logout and callback redirects stay on the site's origin

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-601 · OWASP A01:2021, A01:2025 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any, nextjs, supabase

### Risk

`?next=`, `?redirect_to=` and `?returnTo=` values fed to `redirect()`, `NextResponse.redirect()` or Supabase `redirectTo` send users from a trusted domain to a phishing page; in OAuth or magic-link flows they can carry the auth code off-site. Next.js itself shipped open redirects (CVE-2020-15242, CVE-2021-37699), and Okta documented chaining them with OAuth `redirect_uri` to steal tokens.

### Build rule

Accept only relative destinations: parse with `new URL(next, origin)`, require `url.origin === origin`, then redirect to `url.pathname + url.search`; otherwise fall back to `/`. Never rely on `startsWith('/')`. Keep a fixed allowlist for any absolute destinations. In Supabase Auth settings, set the Site URL and an exact Redirect URLs allowlist (no broad `**` wildcards in production). Exchange the code server-side in `/auth/callback`, then redirect with the same origin check.

### Proof test

1. List every redirect parameter on login, logout, callback and any `/go` route.
2. For each, request with the value `https://asa-probe.invalid/`, then `//asa-probe.invalid`, then `/\asa-probe.invalid`, using `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{redirect_url}'`.
3. Pass: every Location stays on the site's origin. Fail: any Location points to `asa-probe.invalid`.
4. For callbacks that need a valid code, repeat with a test account.

### Sources

- [GHSA-x56p-c8cg-q435 / CVE-2020-15242: Next.js open redirect](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x56p-c8cg-q435)
- [GHSA-vxf5-wxwp-m7g9 / CVE-2021-37699: Next.js open redirect](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vxf5-wxwp-m7g9)
- [Okta Security: Stealing OAuth tokens with open redirects (archived)](https://web.archive.org/web/20250428090710/https://sec.okta.com/articles/2021/02/stealing-oauth-tokens-open-redirects/)

## BROWSER-16 Reset, invite and auth-code URLs do not leak through Referer

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-598, CWE-200 · OWASP A07:2021, A07:2025, API2:2023 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any, supabase

### Risk

Password reset, magic-link, invite and Supabase PKCE `?code=` URLs carry one-time secrets. If the landing page loads third-party resources or the user clicks out before the token is used, the full URL can reach analytics, fonts or chat vendors in the `Referer` header. HackerOne report 272379 (Aspen, 2017) was a reset token leaked this way.

### Build rule

Send `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on auth callback, reset and invite routes (site-wide policy is BROWSER-05). Consume tokens server-side on first hit: the route handler exchanges the code, then redirects to a clean URL. Load no third-party scripts on token-bearing pages.

### Proof test

1. With a test account, request a reset link (or magic link).
2. Open it in a headless browser with network capture.
3. Pass: no third-party request carries the token in `Referer` or its query string, and the final address bar shows no token.
4. Fail: the token appears in any third-party request or stays in the URL after landing.

### Sources

- [HackerOne 272379: Password reset token leak via Referer (mirror)](https://vulners.com/hackerone/H1:272379)
- [thoughtbot: Is your site leaking password reset links?](https://robots.thoughtbot.com/is-your-site-leaking-password-reset-links)
- [OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## BROWSER-17 Auth cookies after login are scoped to the host, not the parent domain

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-1004, CWE-614, CWE-1275 · OWASP A05:2021, A07:2021, A02:2025, A07:2025 · Mode: assisted · Stacks: any, supabase

### Risk

Session cookies set with `Domain=example.com` go to every subdomain, so one compromised or taken-over subdomain can read or overwrite them. `@supabase/ssr` keeps access and refresh tokens readable by JavaScript by design, so any XSS can steal a long-lived refresh token; this raises the stakes of BROWSER-02 and BROWSER-09 rather than being a bug on its own.

### Build rule

App-owned session and CSRF cookies: `__Host-` prefix, `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/`, no `Domain`. Keep Supabase cookie defaults unless all auth is server-side; then document the XSS trade-off and enforce a strict CSP. Never set `Domain` on auth cookies unless subdomain SSO requires it. Never store tokens in `localStorage` as well as cookies. Home-page cookie flags are BROWSER-06.

### Proof test

1. Log in with a test account in headless Playwright (or `curl -sI` the login callback) and capture every `Set-Cookie`.
2. Pass: each auth cookie has `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`, `Path=/`, and no `Domain` (or a documented reason); app-owned session cookies have `HttpOnly`.
3. Report Supabase `sb-*-auth-token` cookies without HttpOnly as informational, linked to the BROWSER-02 result.
4. Fail: missing `Secure`, `SameSite=None` without need, or `Domain=` on a session cookie.

### Sources

- [Supabase docs: Server-side auth advanced guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/server-side/advanced-guide.md)
- [MDN: Set-Cookie](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie)

## BROWSER-18 Third-party scripts are pinned with SRI or inventoried

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-829, CWE-353 · OWASP A08:2021, A03:2025, A08:2025 · Mode: review · Stacks: any, nextjs

### Risk

Every `<script src>` from a CDN or vendor runs with full access to the page, JS-readable cookies and form inputs. In June 2024, after the polyfill.io domain changed owners, `cdn.polyfill.io` served malicious redirects into more than 100,000 sites.

### Build rule

Bundle dependencies from npm instead of runtime CDNs where possible. For pinned, versioned CDN files add `integrity="sha384-..."` and `crossOrigin="anonymous"` (works on `next/script` and `<link>`). For evergreen vendor tags (analytics, chat, scheduling, Stripe.js) where SRI is impossible, keep a written inventory, load them only on pages that need them, keep them off auth, reset and payment-entry pages unless the vendor requires it, and constrain them with CSP `script-src` and `connect-src`. Consider `experimental.sri` for first-party chunks.

### Proof test

1. Fetch each HTML route and list `<script src>` and stylesheet `<link>` tags whose host is not the site's own.
2. Pass: each is versioned with an `integrity` attribute or on the documented vendor inventory, and none come from retired domains such as `polyfill.io`.
3. Optional: a headless page load with request logging catches scripts injected at runtime by tag managers.
4. Fail: unpinned CDN scripts without integrity, or third-party scripts on auth pages not in the inventory.

### Sources

- [BleepingComputer: Polyfill.io JavaScript supply chain attack impacts over 100K sites](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/polyfillio-javascript-supply-chain-attack-impacts-over-100k-sites/)
- [Sonatype: polyfill.io supply chain attack](https://sonatype.com/blog/polyfill.io-supply-chain-attack-hits-100000-websites-all-you-need-to-know)
- [Next.js docs: How to set a Content Security Policy (SRI)](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/content-security-policy)

## BROWSER-19 postMessage listeners check the sender's origin

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-346, CWE-79 · OWASP A01:2021, A03:2021, A01:2025, A05:2025 · Mode: review · Stacks: any

### Risk

`window.addEventListener('message', ...)` accepts messages from any window unless `event.origin` is checked. Apps that embed widgets or are embedded often route message data into navigation, HTML or auth state, and `postMessage(data, '*')` leaks data to whatever page is in the target frame. CVE-2020-8127 (reveal.js) and HackerOne 920285 were DOM XSS through unchecked message handlers.

### Build rule

Every `message` listener checks `event.origin` by exact string equality against an allowlist (no `indexOf`, `includes` or `startsWith`), checks `event.source` when the sender frame is known, validates the message shape with a schema (e.g. zod), and never passes message fields to HTML or URL sinks. Always call `postMessage(data, 'https://exact-origin')`, never `'*'` for anything sensitive. Remove listeners on unmount.

### Proof test

1. Grep the repo for `addEventListener('message'`, `addEventListener("message"`, `onmessage` and `postMessage(`.
2. Pass: each listener has an exact-origin check before it reads `event.data`, and no sensitive `postMessage` uses `'*'`.
3. Fail: any listener uses `event.data` without an exact-origin check, or sensitive data is posted to `'*'`.
4. Optional: from a localhost page that frames or opens the site, post a benign message of the expected shape and confirm the site ignores it.

### Sources

- [GitHub Security Lab issue #118: postMessage missing origin check](https://github.com/github/securitylab/issues/118)
- [jlajara: PostMessage vulnerabilities part II (CVE-2020-8127)](https://jlajara.gitlab.io/Dom_XSS_PostMessage_2)

## BROWSER-20 No mixed content on HTTPS pages

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-319 · OWASP A02:2021, A05:2021, A02:2025, A04:2025 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

An HTTPS page that loads a script, stylesheet, frame or plugin over `http://` is only as safe as that plain-HTTP request: anyone on the network path can replace it and run code in the page. Current browsers block such active mixed content, which breaks the page instead, and upgrade or block mixed images and media. Either way the page is not delivered as written.

### Build rule

Reference every subresource with `https://` or a relative or protocol-relative URL. Do not hard-code `http://` asset hosts in templates, CMS content or environment variables. Add `upgrade-insecure-requests` to the Content-Security-Policy as a safety net for content that editors paste in, and fix the source URLs anyway.

### Proof test

1. The tool crawls the site (same origin only, up to `--max-pages`, default 25) and reads the `src`/`href`/`data` of scripts, stylesheets, frames, objects, images and media on each HTTPS page.
2. Fail: a script, stylesheet, frame, object or embed uses `http://`. Warning: only images or media use `http://`.
3. A page whose CSP has `upgrade-insecure-requests` is listed but not counted, because browsers upgrade its requests.
4. Pass: no `http://` subresource on any crawled page. Not applicable on a plain-HTTP target. Pages behind login are not covered.

### Sources

- [MDN: Mixed content](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Mixed_content)
- [W3C Mixed Content](https://www.w3.org/TR/mixed-content/)

## BROWSER-21 Third-party scripts and styles pinned with Subresource Integrity

Severity: low · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-353, CWE-829 · OWASP A08:2021, A03:2025, A08:2025 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

A script loaded from a CDN or another third party runs with the full power of the page. If that host or the package on it is compromised, the changed file is served to every visitor, and it can read form fields, tokens and session data. Subresource Integrity makes the browser refuse a file whose hash does not match.

### Build rule

Prefer self-hosting libraries through the bundler. When a fixed-version file must come from a CDN, add `integrity="sha384-..."` and `crossorigin="anonymous"` to the `<script>` or `<link rel="stylesheet">`, generated from the exact file. Vendor loaders that change on every release (Stripe.js, Google Tag Manager, reCAPTCHA, Google Fonts CSS) cannot use SRI; allow them by exact host in the CSP instead.

### Proof test

1. The tool crawls the site and collects every `<script src>` and `<link rel="stylesheet">` whose URL is on another origin.
2. Each one must carry an `integrity` attribute. A short list of versionless vendor loaders that cannot use SRI is listed separately and not counted.
3. Pass: every counted third-party script and stylesheet has `integrity`. Warning: one or more do not; the report names them. Not applicable when the crawled pages load no third-party scripts or styles.

### Sources

- [MDN: Subresource Integrity](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Subresource_Integrity)
- [W3C Subresource Integrity](https://www.w3.org/TR/SRI/)

## BROWSER-22 Password forms served and submitted over HTTPS with POST

Severity: high · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-319, CWE-598 · OWASP A02:2021, A07:2021, A04:2025, A07:2025 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

A password typed into a page served over plain HTTP, or sent by a form whose `action` is an `http://` URL, crosses the network in clear text and can be read or changed by anyone on the path, such as a shared Wi-Fi. A login form that uses GET puts the password in the URL, where it is kept in browser history, proxy and server logs and Referer headers.

### Build rule

Serve every page that has a password field over HTTPS only, and give each form a relative or `https://` `action` with `method="post"`. Never point a login form at another host over HTTP. Keep HSTS on (BROWSER-01) so the login page itself cannot be downgraded.

### Proof test

1. The tool crawls the site and records every form that contains `<input type="password">`. Forms are never submitted.
2. Fail: the page is plain HTTP on a non-local host, the form's resolved `action` uses `http://` (except the same local development host), or the form method is not POST.
3. Pass: every password form is on HTTPS (or a local development host, which browsers treat as secure) and posts to HTTPS. Not applicable when no crawled page has a password field; log-in pages that are not linked from public pages need a manual check.

### Sources

- [MDN: Insecure passwords](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Insecure_passwords)
- [OWASP WSTG: Testing for Credentials Transported over an Encrypted Channel](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/04-Authentication_Testing/01-Testing_for_Credentials_Transported_over_an_Encrypted_Channel)

## BROWSER-23 No known-vulnerable client JavaScript libraries

Severity: medium · OSI layer 7 (Application) · CWE-1395, CWE-1104 · OWASP A06:2021, A03:2025 · Mode: auto (proof test built in) · Stacks: any

### Risk

Old copies of popular browser libraries carry published, well-understood bugs: jQuery before 3.5.0 runs scripts hidden in HTML passed to its DOM methods, Bootstrap before 3.4.1 and 4.0 to 4.3.0 allow XSS through tooltip templates, lodash before 4.17.21 allows code injection through `template`, Moment.js before 2.29.4 can be made to hang, and AngularJS 1.x no longer gets fixes at all. Scanners find these versions in seconds.

### Build rule

Install libraries through the package manager and keep them current (`npm outdated`, Dependabot or Renovate). Upgrade jQuery to 3.5.0 or later, Bootstrap to 3.4.1 or 4.3.1 or later, lodash to 4.17.21 or later and Moment.js to 2.29.4 or later (or move to a maintained date library). Migrate AngularJS 1.x apps to a supported framework. Remove copies left in `public/` or `static/` folders.

### Proof test

1. The tool crawls the site, reads the version from script URLs (for example `jquery-3.4.1.min.js`, `/jquery@3.4.1/`, `/ajax/libs/jquery/3.4.1/`) and from the license banner of same-origin scripts. A banner counts only at the start of the library's own header comment (`/*! jQuery v3.4.1`), so a plugin's "Requires jQuery v1.7.2 or later" line is not read as jQuery.
2. It compares against a short embedded list: jQuery < 3.5.0, Bootstrap < 3.4.1 or 4.0.0 to 4.3.0, lodash < 4.17.21, Moment.js < 2.29.4 (fail), AngularJS 1.x (warning, end of life).
3. Pass: no listed library at a vulnerable version is recognised. Bundled code without a banner or version in its URL is not recognised; run `npm audit` on the repository as well.

### Sources

- [OWASP Top 10 2021 A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components](https://owasp.org/Top10/A06_2021-Vulnerable_and_Outdated_Components/)
- [NVD CVE-2020-11022 (jQuery)](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-11022)
- [NVD CVE-2019-8331 (Bootstrap)](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-8331)
- [NVD CVE-2021-23337 (lodash)](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-23337)
- [NVD CVE-2022-31129 (Moment.js)](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-31129)
- [AngularJS version support status](https://docs.angularjs.org/misc/version-support-status)
